data_and_models: Nothing is trained. Two model call sites and only two - Gemini 3.7 Flash and 3.5 Flash via the Google GenAI SDK on Vertex AI for rulebook extraction and for writing the sentence a human hears on the phone - with the observation and decision path deliberately model-free: Watch makes zero model calls and the state machine is a pure function, on the stated principle that control flow a model can talk itself out of is not control flow. Intake's second pass may structure only what its first pass extracted, which is what makes an invented requirement traceable, and every requirement carries the source wording it came from. Infrastructure: Cloud Run, Cloud Scheduler, Firestore, FastAPI, Docker, Twilio voice. One deployment fact is recorded as forced: Vertex in the global region while Firestore sits in nam5, because no Gemini 3.x model was available in us-central1, discovered by probing every model in every region rather than reading a model list. What is measured is extraction against a 29-obligation key; no accuracy, false-positive or missed-check figure is published for the checker itself, which is the part that phones you.
name: Tower

numbers.arithmetic: reproduces: each published F1 equals 2PR/(P+R) to the decimal shown (73.49, 88.86, 84.31), and each recall times 29 gives an exact integer count of matched obligations (18.01, 27.00, 23.00), so recall is checkable against the stated key. Precision is not: the extraction counts its denominators would need are 20.01 for run 1 - an integer, so that run is coherent - but 31.76 and 25.55 for runs 2 and 3, which no integer number of extractions can produce, and the page never publishes how many requirements each run extracted. The honest reading is that recall and F1 are audited figures and precision is a summary number whose denominator was left out.
numbers.claim: extraction scored three times against a 29-obligation key: 62.1/90.0 (F1 73.5), 93.1/85.0 (F1 88.9), 79.3/90.0 (F1 84.3)
numbers.denominator: 29 hand-written ground-truth obligations from the official rules

numbers.arithmetic: not falsifiable from the page: neither plausible population yields an integer - 96% of the 23 matched obligations is 22.08 and of all 29 is 27.84; 91% is 20.93 and 26.39 - so the two agreements cannot be attributed to a count and no error budget is attached to the fields (severity, class) that decide whether the phone rings

contradicted by the page's own stated cadence: every thirty minutes is 48 ticks a day, not 96; 96 is what a fifteen-minute schedule would give. The guard's necessity is unaffected - one call per tick per open finding is still dozens a day - but this is the one figure on the page that its own inputs refute, and it is quoted here rather than smoothed over
numbers.claim: a thirty-minute schedule without the idempotency guard 'phones you ninety six times a day about the same missing file'
numbers.denominator: ticks per day at the stated schedule

numbers.arithmetic: not falsifiable from the page after the fix: it is a post-mortem count with no artifact to re-check, but it is internally coherent (12 requirements, slug-keyed routes, two surviving a rename) and it is the only quantification given for the failure mode that motivated routing on content
numbers.claim: 9 of 12 requirements silently lost their tool surface when IDs were unstable
numbers.denominator: requirements in the routing table for that run

numbers.arithmetic: structural: every input to the table is stated, so a reader can reproduce the behaviour from the description alone (and 48 evaluations a day at the stated cadence). Nothing about accuracy depends on it - the thresholds are a judgement about how much warning a deadline needs
numbers.claim: escalation policy: Kill requirements call immediately, Major wait until seven days out, Minor never call; re-checks every thirty minutes

numbers.arithmetic: structural: a coverage report, self-consistent as 5/10 with 5 named as unverifiable, but no run id or rulebook is attached, so it cannot be tied to any of the three scored extraction runs - and it is the only number on the page that describes the checker rather than the extractor
numbers.claim: 'Tower says it verified five of ten applicable requirements and names the five it could not'
numbers.denominator: applicable requirements for the run being described

one_line: A watchstander for competition rules: it extracts every obligation from a rulebook verbatim, gives each one a severity and a named place to look for evidence, re-checks the live repository, URLs and video every thirty minutes for weeks, and keeps RESOLVED, RETRACTED and UNVERIFIED as three different answers so that 'I could not see' can never read as an all clear.

sections.accomplishments: The author scored their own extraction and published the number that came back, against a hand-written ground-truth key of 29 obligations from the official rules. Three runs, and the movement is the substance: run 1 baseline 62.1% recall / 90.0% precision / F1 73.5; run 2 93.1 / 85.0 / 88.9 after finding a bug in the scorer itself, which consumed each requirement once so a single requirement covering three bundled obligations scored two as missed; run 3 the figure they call honest, 79.3 / 90.0 / 84.3, after auditing the matched pairs by eye and catching four false credits caused by loose keywords, then revising the scorer against themselves. Also published: 96% severity agreement and 91% class agreement. The misses have a shape rather than being random - all three missed disqualifying requirements are standing conditions and legal clauses (the submission window, no-edits-after-deadline, original work ownership) while zero artifact requirements were missed (it found the video, the diagram, the README, the repository, the description, the category and the tech stack) - and the explanation is volunteered against the author's own design: the class taxonomy pushes toward 'what must the entrant DO' and deduplication folds adjacent legal language together, so a watchstander built to answer 'is the work ready' is structurally weaker at 'is the entrant eligible'. The stated fix is a separate eligibility pass rather than prompt tuning. Separately: a 32-assertion offline harness covering the state machine including both reversal paths, the escalation policy including idempotency, checker honesty and login-wall detection, which runs in about a second with no credentials and no cost, so - in the author's words - it can be re-run rather than believed.
sections.challenges: Eight defects are listed, and the page's own reading is that they are the same bug wearing different hats: the system claiming knowledge it did not have. (1) Requirement IDs were unstable across extraction runs - the same obligation came back as `spinup-instructions-readme` one run and `spin-up-instructions` the next, and because the routing table keyed off those slugs, 9 of 12 requirements silently lost their tool surface and reported as unverifiable; routes now match on content, since content survives re-extraction and model-generated slugs do not. (2) Blank configuration read as failure - an unset URL reported UNMET rather than UNCHECKED, one tick from phoning the author at three in the morning about its own empty config file. (3) Expired credentials retried silently for five minutes and then died, which for a scheduled unattended agent is indistinguishable from a tick that found nothing wrong: silence meant both 'all clear' and 'I am broken'. (4) Conditional requirements were checked unconditionally - the rules say *if* the hosted site is private *then* supply credentials, Tower dropped the 'if' and the model invented the premise, narrating a private website that does not exist; declared facts now default to false so an unknown premise is never assumed true. (5) Narration was tied to state changes, so on the one tick where a call actually went out the requirement was already open, nothing changed, no sentence was generated, and Twilio read a raw Python fallback string down the phone line, list brackets included. (6) Tower apologised for a call it never made - it reversed a finding that had never been escalated and said 'please disregard our previous alert' when there had been none; call history is now an input to narration. (7) A dry run mutated state, resolving a pending finding and silently consuming it; dry runs are read-only. (8) The worst: Tower reported a requirement SATISFIED on the strength of words appearing on Devpost's login page - an unsubmitted draft redirects anonymous visitors to sign-in, that page returns HTTP 200, the status check believed it had fetched the project and pattern-matched against a login form; 'A 200 is not the same as reaching the thing you asked for.' There is now a login-wall detector with a regression test pinning it. The page then adds the finding that matters most for how to read the rest of it: the eval harness was green the entire time defect 8 existed, so thirty passing assertions proved the logic was correct and proved nothing about whether the logic could run on real input.
sections.how_we_built_it: Four agents under deterministic control flow. Intake reads the rulebook in two passes: pass one extracts obligation statements verbatim with no interpretation, pass two structures only what pass one found, so an invented requirement has nowhere to come from, and every requirement keeps the words it came from - which is what makes hallucination checkable 'in seconds'. Watch observes and nothing else: it makes zero model calls, mapping requirements to real tool surfaces (files in the live GitHub repo, public URLs, YouTube oEmbed, the Devpost project page) and reporting what it saw. Analyst decides what an observation means, with the state machine written as a pure function so a model never decides whether to escalate. Escalation is a policy table rather than a judgement: Kill requirements call immediately, Major wait until seven days out, Minor never call, and every call is idempotent because a thirty-minute schedule without that guard would phone about the same missing file repeatedly. Gemini is used in exactly two places - extracting the rulebook and writing the sentence a human hears - with the stated principle that control flow a model can talk itself out of is not control flow. Stack: Gemini 3.7 Flash and 3.5 Flash through the Google GenAI SDK on Vertex AI, Cloud Run, Cloud Scheduler, Firestore, Twilio for voice, Docker, FastAPI, Python. One architecture decision is recorded as forced rather than chosen: Vertex runs in the global region while Firestore sits in nam5, because no Gemini 3.x model was available in us-central1 for this project - found by writing a script that tries every candidate model in every region and prints what actually answers, rather than trusting a model list.
sections.inspiration: The author is a former Navy air traffic controller, and the metaphor is carried through literally: the job was watching things that only go wrong when nobody is looking and deciding which of forty items on a scope matters right now. The personal setup is fourteen builds and six deadlines running at once, where 'every one of them has a rulebook, and every rulebook has a clause that will disqualify you quietly' - the clause being boring rather than hard: a video set to unlisted instead of public, a repository nobody shared, a category never selected on a form. The diagnosis is that nobody loses a competition because the idea was bad; they lose because at eleven at night on the last day one box was unticked and there was no one on watch. So the project is 'the watchstander'.
sections.learned: A monitoring agent's hardest problem is not detection, it is knowing what it does not know - and every defect in the build is named as a variant of that: a 200 status code that was really a login wall, an unset variable that looked like failure, an expired credential that looked like silence, a conditional whose premise got invented to fill the gap. In each case, the page says, the system had an honest answer available ('I cannot tell') and reached for a confident one instead. The author is explicit that this is not a Gemini problem but a design problem, and that the fix is boring and structural: make 'unknown' a first-class value that propagates, refuse to let a checker return a boolean when it has not actually checked, and report coverage out loud so the gap is visible instead of implied. The closing claim is that Tower says it verified five of ten applicable requirements and names the five it could not - 'a worse-looking number than implying it checked everything, and the only number worth trusting'.
sections.what_it_does: Tower reads a competition rulebook once and turns it into a set of machine-checkable requirements, each carrying a severity and a specific place to look for evidence, then runs every thirty minutes for weeks, unattended, checking the live repository, public URLs and the video against that set. When something crosses the line it does not send an email: it calls the entrant's phone and says in one sentence what is about to disqualify them and how long they have. The part the author rates more highly is the reversal - when the problem is fixed, Tower calls back and stands its own alert down, and when it was wrong to call at all, it says so, because most verification agents only ever add findings. Three states carry that distinction and are explicitly not the same admission: RESOLVED (called, problem was real, fixed), RETRACTED (called, and the evidence was already in place - Tower was wrong), UNVERIFIED (could not actually check; 'Not satisfied. Not unmet. Unknown.'). The page names that third state as the spine of the system, with the reasoning that an agent which cannot distinguish 'everything is fine' from 'I could not see' is worse than no agent, because silence reads as an all clear.
sections.what_next: Four items, the first of which follows from the measured weakness rather than from ambition: a separate eligibility pass, because the misses are standing conditions and the fix belongs in architecture rather than prompt tuning. More rulebooks - the code is already not specific to this competition, and 'a watchstander tracking one deadline is a timer; tracking six is a watch'. Rule-change detection, so an amended rulebook makes Tower notice its own requirement set is stale and re-extract instead of confidently watching yesterday's rules. And a fail-fast heartbeat: if the scheduler stops firing, Tower calls to say it has stopped watching, because 'an agent that notices its own absence is the version I actually want on the scope'.

testing: Two separate things, and the page is candid that they cover different ground. An eval: extraction scored against a hand-written ground-truth key of 29 obligations from the official rules, run three times, with recall, precision and F1 published for each run and the reason for each movement stated (a scorer bug, then four false credits found by auditing matched pairs by eye), plus 96% severity and 91% class agreement. A harness: 32 offline assertions over the state machine including both reversal paths, the escalation policy including idempotency, checker honesty and login-wall detection, running in about a second with no credentials. And one honest negative result that outweighs both: the harness was green for the entire period in which the login-wall defect existed, so thirty passing assertions proved the logic was correct and proved nothing about whether the logic could run on real input. No repository is linked, so neither suite can be read or re-run from here - the numbers are the author's, and only the F1 arithmetic is independently checkable.
